items.classSummary: Session 1: Why corporates and startups need each other. Corporates have money, distribution, brand, data and regulatory know-how but move slowly and struggle to innovate outside their core. Startups have speed, focus and new technology but lack customers, capital and credibility. Collaboration tries to combine the two. We discussed the 'dinosaur and the mouse' asymmetry and why most collaborations fail on mismatched expectations rather than technology.
items.unclearQuestion: Okay maybe this is a silly one — if the big company has all the money and engineers, why can't it just copy the startup's idea instead of partnering? Is that even allowed?? And why would a startup ever risk showing them anything?
keyPoints: Corporates bring capital, distribution, brand, data and regulatory know-how but innovate slowly outside their core
Startups bring speed, focus and new technology but lack customers, capital and credibility
Collaboration aims to combine these complementary strengths
Most collaborations fail on mismatched expectations rather than on the technology
items.tutorReply: Not silly at all — it's the question every founder secretly asks! Legally, a corporate can build something similar unless it's protected by patents, trade secrets or a signed NDA. Practically, copying is harder than it looks: the startup's real edge is often speed, a team that has lived the problem for years, and hundreds of small learnings that aren't visible in a demo. Big firms also face internal hurdles — budgets, competing priorities, risk committees — so building in-house can take 2–3 years, while partnering can take months. That's why many corporates would rather pilot, invest or acquire. Startups protect themselves by sharing the 'what' before the 'how', using NDAs, and choosing partners with a track record of fair dealing.
followUps: What exactly should a startup NOT show in a first meeting with a corporate?
Has a big company ever been caught copying a startup after a pilot?
If copying is so hard, why do corporates still have big R&D labs?

thread.question: What exactly should a startup NOT show in a first meeting with a corporate? Like, can I show my code? My customer list? My pricing??
thread.tutorReply: Great instinct to ask before the meeting rather than after! In a first meeting, share the problem you solve, outcomes ("we cut onboarding time by 40% for a bank"), and a demo of the product's behaviour. Hold back source code, model weights or architecture details, your full customer list and contract terms, and anything that reveals how you achieve the result. Pricing can be shared as a range. A simple rule: show what the corporate needs to decide whether to continue the conversation, and nothing more. Deeper technical disclosure should wait for a mutual NDA and a clear use case — which is a big theme in Session 9.
followUps: Is a mutual NDA actually enforceable against a huge company?
How do I demo an AI product without revealing how it works?

items.text: Random thought after Session 1: if the dinosaur and mouse need each other, who should make the first move? Do startups cold-email corporates, or do corporates have scouting teams? Bringing this to next class.

items.classSummary: Session 2: Open innovation. Henry Chesbrough's idea that firms should use external as well as internal ideas and paths to market. Outside-in: bringing external knowledge in (licensing, partnerships, crowdsourcing). Inside-out: letting unused internal ideas go out (spin-offs, out-licensing). Coupled: co-creation with partners. Examples included P&G's Connect + Develop and corporates licensing idle patents.
items.unclearQuestion: If open innovation means sharing ideas with outsiders, doesn't the company just... lose its secrets? How is 'open' different from 'giving stuff away for free'? Also is open innovation the same as open source?
keyPoints: Open innovation means using external as well as internal ideas and paths to market
Outside-in brings external knowledge in through licensing, partnerships and crowdsourcing
Inside-out lets unused internal ideas out through spin-offs and out-licensing
Coupled innovation is co-creation with partners, e.g. P&G's Connect + Develop
items.tutorReply: Love this — you've spotted the tension at the heart of the idea! 'Open' doesn't mean free; it means the company stops assuming every good idea must be invented and commercialised inside its own walls. Ideas flow both ways, but usually through contracts: licences, revenue shares, equity in spin-offs. P&G didn't give its secrets away — it published problems it wanted solved and paid outsiders who solved them. Inside-out is often about monetising patents that would otherwise sit unused. And no, it's not the same as open source: open source is a licensing model where code is publicly available; open innovation is a broader strategy that can be fully proprietary. They can overlap, but one is a business strategy and the other is a way of licensing.
followUps: How does a company decide which ideas are 'core' and must stay closed?
Can a startup be the inside-out spin-off of a corporate? How does that work?
Is posting a problem on a crowdsourcing site risky for the company?

items.classSummary: Session 3: The engagement spectrum. Corporates can engage startups in many ways, from light-touch to deep commitment: events and hackathons, innovation challenges, pilots and proofs of concept, venture clienting (buying the startup's product), accelerator programmes, corporate venture capital investment, and finally M&A. Each mode differs in cost, control, speed and risk. Companies often use several at once.
items.unclearQuestion: Why do corporates bother with hackathons at all? Isn't it just free pizza and marketing? Also — how do they decide whether to just buy the product vs invest vs acquire the whole startup? Is there like a flowchart?
keyPoints: Corporates engage startups across a spectrum from light-touch to deep commitment
Modes include events and hackathons, challenges, pilots, venture clienting, accelerators, CVC and M&A
Each mode differs in cost, control, speed and risk
Companies often run several engagement modes at the same time
items.tutorReply: Ha — sometimes it is mostly pizza and marketing! But good hackathons do real work: they scout talent and startups cheaply, test whether internal data or APIs are usable by outsiders, and signal to the ecosystem that the company is open to partners. There's no single official flowchart, but a useful rule of thumb: if you mainly need the solution, buy it (venture clienting or a pilot). If you want a window on a market and the option to go deeper later, invest a minority stake (CVC). If the capability is strategic and you need control, acquire. Cost and commitment rise as you move along that spectrum, so firms usually start light and move deeper only when evidence justifies it.
followUps: Has a hackathon ever led to a real acquisition?
What's the risk if a corporate jumps straight to acquiring a startup?
Can a startup say no to an investment but yes to being a supplier?

thread.question: Can a startup say no to an investment but yes to being a supplier? Wouldn't the corporate get offended lol
thread.tutorReply: Absolutely they can — and many smart founders do! Taking a corporate's money can create signalling problems: competitors of that corporate may refuse to buy from you, and later investors may worry the corporate has special rights. Being a supplier keeps you neutral. Professional corporate teams understand this; the ones who get offended are usually telling you something about how the partnership would go. The polite path is to say: "We'd love to earn your business as a customer first, and revisit investment once we've proven value together." That keeps the door open without locking you in.
followUps: What special rights do corporate investors usually ask for?
Do startups ever regret NOT taking corporate money?

items.classSummary: Session 4: Corporate accelerators and incubators. Corporates run time-bound programmes (usually 3–6 months) that give cohorts of startups mentoring, access to business units, data and sometimes funding, often in exchange for equity or first rights to partner. Incubators work with earlier-stage ideas over longer periods. We compared equity-based and equity-free models and discussed why many corporate accelerators shut down within a few years.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would a startup give up equity just for 'mentoring'? Couldn't they just watch YouTube? And if so many corporate accelerators shut down, is it a red flag to join one?
keyPoints: Corporate accelerators are time-bound programmes of roughly 3–6 months for startup cohorts
They offer mentoring, access to business units and data, and sometimes funding
Startups often give equity or first partnership rights in return
Incubators work with earlier-stage ideas over longer periods
Equity-based and equity-free models differ, and many corporate accelerators close within a few years
items.tutorReply: The YouTube comparison is hilarious and kind of fair! Generic mentoring is cheap. What startups actually pay for in a good corporate accelerator is access: a named business-unit sponsor, real data to test on, procurement fast-tracks, and a credible logo for the next sales pitch. If a programme can't show that access, giving up equity is a bad deal — which is why equity-free models have grown. As for closures: it's not automatically a red flag, but check three things before joining — is there a business-unit sponsor with budget, how many past startups got paid contracts, and does the programme report to someone senior? Programmes that are only an innovation-theatre marketing exercise are the ones that disappear.
followUps: What does 'innovation theatre' actually look like from the inside?
How much equity is normal for a corporate accelerator to take?
Can a startup join two competing corporates' accelerators?

items.text: Wait, if equity-free accelerators exist, how does the corporate make money from them? Guessing it's first look at partnerships + PR? Need to check before Session 5 on CVC.

items.classSummary: Session 5: Corporate venture capital. CVC units invest corporate money in external startups, usually minority stakes. Objectives can be strategic (window on technology, new markets, complementary products) or financial (returns), and most CVCs try to balance both. We looked at how strategic CVCs judge success differently from independent VCs and at examples like Intel Capital and Google Ventures.
items.unclearQuestion: Super basic question but — if the CVC is investing the company's own money, why does it matter whether it makes a profit? Isn't the 'strategic' part the whole point? Who even decides if a CVC was successful?
keyPoints: CVC units invest corporate money in external startups, usually as minority stakes
Objectives can be strategic (technology window, new markets, complementary products) or financial
Most CVCs try to balance strategic and financial goals
Strategic CVCs judge success differently from independent VCs, e.g. Intel Capital and Google Ventures
items.tutorReply: Basic questions are where the real understanding lives! Profit matters for two reasons. First, credibility: a CVC that loses money is easy for the CFO to shut down in a bad year, so financial returns protect the strategic mission. Second, discipline: chasing 'strategic value' without return expectations can lead to overpaying for fashionable startups. Who decides success? Usually a mix: the CVC's investment committee, the business units it's meant to serve, and the CFO. Good CVCs agree up front on strategic metrics — like the number of portfolio startups that become suppliers or partners — alongside financial ones such as IRR, so success isn't judged purely on vibes after the fact.
followUps: What happens to portfolio startups when a corporate shuts its CVC?
Why would a startup prefer a CVC over a normal VC?
How is a CVC partner paid compared to a regular VC partner?

thread.question: What happens to portfolio startups when a corporate shuts its CVC? Do they have to give the money back?? 😅
thread.tutorReply: No refunds, don't worry 😄 The investment is equity, so the startup keeps the cash and the corporate keeps its shares. What usually happens is less dramatic but still painful: the corporate stops making follow-on investments, the board seat may go quiet, and the internal champions who connected the startup to business units move on. Sometimes the corporate sells the whole portfolio to a secondary buyer. That's why founders ask how long a CVC has existed, whether it has its own committed fund, and whether it has survived a downturn before — topics we'll see in Session 6 on structures and governance.
followUps: What is a 'secondary buyer' for a portfolio?
Does a dedicated fund really protect startups better than balance-sheet investing?

items.classSummary: Session 6: CVC structures and governance. CVCs can invest directly from the balance sheet, through a dedicated fund with committed capital, or as a limited partner in an external VC fund. We discussed investment committees, how independent the CVC team should be from business units, compensation (carry vs salary/bonus), and how structure affects speed of decision-making and longevity.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would a corporate put its money into someone else's VC fund instead of investing directly? Feels like paying someone to do your homework. And what does 'carry' actually mean — is it literally carrying the profits?
keyPoints: CVCs can invest from the balance sheet, through a dedicated fund, or as an LP in an external VC fund
Investment committees and the CVC team's independence from business units shape governance
Compensation can be carry-based or salary-and-bonus
Structure affects decision speed and how long the CVC survives
items.tutorReply: 'Paying someone to do your homework' is honestly a decent description — and sometimes it's smart! Investing as an LP in an external fund lets a corporate learn the market, see a wide deal flow and build relationships without hiring a full investment team. It's often a first step before setting up its own CVC. And 'carry' (carried interest) is the share of investment profits — typically around 20% — paid to the people managing the fund once investors get their money back. Many CVCs don't offer carry and pay salary plus bonus instead, which makes it harder to retain experienced VCs. That's one reason dedicated, more independent fund structures tend to attract better investors and last longer.
followUps: Why don't more corporates just give their CVC team carry?
How fast can a balance-sheet CVC actually sign a deal?
Who sits on a typical CVC investment committee?

items.classSummary: Session 7: Venture clienting, pilots and proofs of concept. Venture clienting means the corporate becomes a paying customer of the startup instead of an investor. Pilots and POCs test a solution on a small scale. Many collaborations get stuck in 'pilot purgatory' — endless unpaid or small pilots that never scale. We covered success criteria, paid pilots, business-unit ownership and a defined path to a full contract.
items.unclearQuestion: Why would anyone agree to an UNPAID pilot? Isn't that just free consulting for a billion-dollar company? And how many pilots is too many before a startup should walk away?
keyPoints: Venture clienting means the corporate becomes a paying customer rather than an investor
Pilots and proofs of concept test a solution at small scale
Many collaborations get stuck in 'pilot purgatory' and never scale
Clear success criteria, paid pilots, business-unit ownership and a path to contract help avoid it
items.tutorReply: Your outrage is very valid! Early-stage startups accept unpaid pilots because the logo, the reference and the real-world data can be worth a lot — but only if there's a clear path to a contract. The warning signs of pilot purgatory: no named business-unit owner with budget, no written success criteria, and 'let's extend the pilot' after the pilot has already succeeded. A good rule: agree in writing before starting what result triggers a paid rollout. As for 'how many is too many' — if a second pilot with the same corporate is proposed without new learning goals, or a pilot runs past about 3–6 months without a purchase decision, it's time to push for a contract or walk away.
followUps: How do you price a paid pilot without scaring the corporate off?
What should the written success criteria actually look like?
Can a startup charge for a pilot after doing a free one already?

thread.question: What should the written success criteria actually look like? Like literally, what do I write on the page?
thread.tutorReply: Love the 'literally' — let's make it concrete! A one-page pilot charter usually has: (1) the business problem in the corporate's words; (2) 2–3 measurable targets, e.g. 'reduce invoice-processing time from 5 days to 2 for 500 invoices'; (3) the baseline and how it's measured, and by whom; (4) duration and the data or systems access the startup gets; (5) named owners on both sides; and (6) the decision trigger: 'If targets are met, the business unit will start procurement for a rollout of X within 30 days.' Both sides sign it. That last line is the anti-purgatory clause — it turns a 'nice experiment' into a commitment.
followUps: Who on the corporate side should sign the pilot charter?
What if the corporate keeps changing the targets mid-pilot?

items.text: Group discussion: we argued about whether pilot purgatory is the corporate's fault or the startup's. Harry says corporates, Naman says startups who don't ask for a contract. I think it's both? Asking in Session 8.

items.classSummary: Session 8: Global Capability Centres (GCCs) in India. Multinationals run GCCs in cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurugram, which have evolved from back-office cost centres into hubs for engineering, R&D and product innovation. Many GCCs now run startup engagement programmes, partner with local startups and act as a bridge between Indian startups and global headquarters.
items.unclearQuestion: Is a GCC basically just an outsourcing office with a fancier name? And if a startup partners with a GCC in Bengaluru, does that actually reach the global HQ, or does it stay stuck in India?
keyPoints: Multinationals run GCCs in Indian cities such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune and Gurugram
GCCs have evolved from back-office cost centres into hubs for engineering, R&D and product innovation
Many GCCs now run startup engagement programmes and partner with local startups
GCCs can act as a bridge between Indian startups and global headquarters
items.tutorReply: That's exactly how GCCs were seen 15–20 years ago! The difference from outsourcing: a GCC is owned by the multinational itself, so its people are employees working on the company's own products, not a vendor's. Many now own global products or platforms end to end. Whether a startup partnership reaches HQ depends on the GCC's mandate. Ask: does this GCC own a global product line or budget? Is there a named global sponsor? Has a previous startup partner been rolled out in other countries? When the answer is yes, the GCC is a fantastic, accessible entry point — same time zone, local leadership, faster meetings. When the answer is no, the partnership risks becoming a local showcase.
followUps: How does a startup find out which GCC teams own global budgets?
Do GCCs pay Indian startups in rupees or dollars?
Are GCC startup programmes different from corporate accelerators?

items.classSummary: Session 9: Legal foundations. We went through the main documents in corporate-startup deals: NDAs (mutual vs one-way), term sheets for investments, master services agreements (MSAs) and statements of work for supplier relationships, plus clauses on exclusivity, rights of first refusal, liability and termination. Startups often lack legal resources and sign standard corporate templates without negotiating.
items.unclearQuestion: Maybe dumb but — if the corporate's lawyers write the contract, isn't it always going to be unfair to the startup? Can a tiny startup really negotiate with a giant legal team? What's the ONE clause we should never sign blindly?
keyPoints: Core documents include NDAs, investment term sheets, MSAs and statements of work
NDAs can be mutual or one-way
Key clauses cover exclusivity, rights of first refusal, liability and termination
Startups often sign standard corporate templates without negotiating
items.tutorReply: Not dumb — this is the question that saves startups! Corporate templates are written to protect the corporate, but they're usually a starting point, not a final offer. Small startups negotiate successfully all the time by being specific: instead of 'this is unfair', say 'we can accept this liability cap at the contract value, not unlimited'. If I had to pick one clause never to sign blindly, it's exclusivity (and its cousin, the right of first refusal). Exclusivity can stop you selling to a whole industry, and a ROFR can scare off future acquirers. Close runners-up: unlimited liability and IP assignment clauses — which we'll unpack properly in Session 10.
followUps: When does it actually make sense to give a corporate exclusivity?
How much does it cost a startup to get a lawyer to review an MSA?
What's the difference between a one-way and mutual NDA in practice?

thread.question: When does it actually make sense to give a corporate exclusivity? Is it ever a good deal or always a trap?
thread.tutorReply: Not always a trap — it's a trade, so price it like one! Exclusivity can make sense when it is narrow, short and paid for: limited to one product category or region, for around 12–18 months, and in exchange for a guaranteed minimum purchase or meaningful revenue. Add a 'use it or lose it' condition: if the corporate doesn't hit agreed volumes, exclusivity ends automatically. What you should avoid is broad, open-ended exclusivity given away for free just to land a famous logo. Ask yourself: if this partner went quiet for a year, could my company survive with this clause in place?
followUps: What's a 'minimum purchase commitment' and how is it enforced?
Can exclusivity be cancelled early if the corporate breaks the deal?

items.classSummary: Session 10: IP risks. Background IP is what each party brings into the collaboration; foreground IP is what is created during it. Joint development raises questions about ownership, licensing rights, field-of-use restrictions and what happens when the partnership ends. We discussed cases where startups lost rights to their core technology through broad IP assignment clauses, and how licences can be used instead of assignment.
items.unclearQuestion: If my startup and a corporate build something together, who owns it — is it split 50/50 like a group project? And what happens if the corporate 'improves' our tech — do they own our tech now??
keyPoints: Background IP is what each party brings; foreground IP is created during the collaboration
Joint development raises questions about ownership, licensing, field-of-use and post-partnership rights
Broad IP assignment clauses have cost startups the rights to their core technology
Licences can be used instead of assignment to protect the startup
items.tutorReply: The group-project comparison is perfect — and just like group projects, the default often isn't 50/50! Who owns foreground IP depends entirely on the contract. Without careful drafting, joint ownership can be messy: in some jurisdictions each co-owner can exploit it without the other's consent. A common, startup-friendly structure is: each side keeps its background IP; the startup owns improvements to its own core technology; the corporate owns things specific to its business (like integrations with its internal systems); and the corporate gets a licence to use what it needs. If the corporate 'improves' your tech under a broad assignment clause, they could own those improvements — which is exactly why you negotiate the clause before you write any code together.
followUps: What's a field-of-use restriction, in simple words?
How do we prove what our 'background IP' was before the project started?
Can a corporate patent something we built together without telling us?

items.text: Note for the group: background vs foreground IP is going to be on the exam for sure. Silly memory trick — background = what you bring from home, foreground = what you make in class.

items.classSummary: Session 11: Cultural gaps. Corporates and startups differ in speed, risk appetite, decision rights, planning horizons and attitude to failure. Corporate procurement, compliance and security reviews can take months, which can kill a startup's cash runway. We discussed boundary spanners, fast-track procurement and 'translators' who help both sides understand each other.
items.unclearQuestion: Why do corporates take 6 months to sign a purchase order for something that costs less than their coffee budget? Is it really culture, or are they just being lazy? Also what does a 'boundary spanner' actually do all day?
keyPoints: Corporates and startups differ in speed, risk appetite, decision rights, planning horizons and attitude to failure
Procurement, compliance and security reviews can take months and drain a startup's runway
Boundary spanners and 'translators' help each side understand the other
Fast-track procurement can reduce delays
items.tutorReply: The coffee-budget comparison made me laugh — and it's painfully accurate! It's rarely laziness. Corporate processes are built to manage risk at scale: a security review exists because one weak supplier can cause a breach affecting millions of customers, and procurement rules exist to prevent fraud and favouritism. The problem is that the same heavy process is applied to a ₹5 lakh pilot and a ₹500 crore contract. A boundary spanner is the person who lives between the two worlds: they translate startup urgency into corporate language (risk, compliance, ROI), find the right approver, pre-fill security questionnaires with the startup, and push for fast-track procurement. On a good day they save the startup months; on a bad day they're chasing signatures!
followUps: How can a startup speed up a security review from its own side?
Is a boundary spanner usually from the corporate or the startup?
What is 'fast-track procurement' and who is allowed to approve it?

thread.question: How can a startup speed up a security review from its own side? Like is there a cheat code?
thread.tutorReply: There's no cheat code, but there's definitely a speed-run strategy! Prepare a security pack before anyone asks: a filled-in standard questionnaire, your data-flow diagram, where data is stored, encryption details, access controls and incident-response process. If you can afford it, certifications like ISO 27001 or a SOC 2 report answer most questions at once. Offer a short call between your tech lead and their security team early — many weeks are lost to back-and-forth emails. Finally, scope the pilot to minimise risk: anonymised or synthetic data, no production access. A lower-risk pilot often qualifies for a lighter review.
followUps: How expensive is it for a startup to get ISO 27001 or SOC 2?
What's the difference between anonymised and synthetic data?

items.classSummary: Session 12: Partnership pitfalls. Common reasons collaborations fail: misaligned KPIs and incentives, the internal champion leaving or changing role, not-invented-here syndrome among corporate engineers, startups becoming dependent on one big customer, and unclear ownership after a pilot. We discussed warning signs and ways to de-risk each pitfall.
items.unclearQuestion: What happens if the one person at the corporate who loves our startup just... quits? Does the whole partnership die? That seems like a really fragile way to run a business. And is 'not-invented-here' actually a real thing or just an excuse?
keyPoints: Misaligned KPIs and incentives commonly cause collaborations to fail
Losing the internal champion through a role change or exit can stall a partnership
Not-invented-here syndrome among corporate engineers creates resistance
Dependence on one big customer and unclear post-pilot ownership are major risks
items.tutorReply: This fear is completely justified — champion loss is one of the most common reasons partnerships die! The fix is to never have just one champion. From day one, build relationships at three levels: the day-to-day user, the business-unit budget owner, and an executive sponsor. Get success written down in shared documents and dashboards, so the value survives a reshuffle. And when a champion leaves, ask them to introduce you to their successor before they go. Not-invented-here is very real: engineers can see an external solution as a threat to their jobs or pride. You counter it by involving internal teams early, giving them credit, and positioning the startup as a tool that makes them look good, not as a replacement.
followUps: How do you approach an executive sponsor without going over your champion's head?
What share of revenue from one customer is 'too dependent'?
Can not-invented-here ever be a good thing for the corporate?

items.classSummary: Session 13: Designing and measuring partnerships, and course wrap-up. We pulled the course together: choose the engagement mode to fit the strategic goal, agree KPIs that matter to both sides (for example time-to-contract, adoption, revenue and learning), plan integration early, and define exit or scale-up paths in advance. We revisited open innovation, CVC, GCCs, legal and IP risks, cultural gaps and pitfalls as one connected framework.
items.unclearQuestion: Okay big-picture silly question: after 13 sessions, is corporate-startup collaboration actually worth it, or does it mostly fail? If we were founders tomorrow, should we even try partnering with a big company?
keyPoints: Choose the engagement mode to fit the strategic goal
Agree KPIs that matter to both sides, such as time-to-contract, adoption, revenue and learning
Plan integration early and define exit or scale-up paths in advance
Open innovation, CVC, GCCs, legal and IP risks, cultural gaps and pitfalls form one connected framework
items.tutorReply: What a perfect question to end the course with! Honestly: many individual collaborations do fail, but the ones that work can be transformational — a single corporate customer or partner can give a startup distribution it would take years to build alone. The course's real lesson is that success isn't luck; it's design. If you were founders tomorrow, I'd say yes, try — but go in with your eyes open: pick partners with a track record, start with a paid, well-scoped pilot with written success criteria, protect your IP and avoid broad exclusivity, build several champions, and never let one corporate be more than a large slice of your revenue. Do that, and you're already ahead of most founders who walk into these deals.
followUps: If you had to pick only one lesson from all 13 sessions, which would it be?
What kind of startup should probably NOT partner with corporates?
How would we design our own final project as a corporate-startup partnership?

thread.question: If you had to pick only one lesson from all 13 sessions, which would it be?
thread.tutorReply: Tough one — but I'd pick: agree, in writing, what success looks like before you start. It quietly solves problems from almost every session. It prevents pilot purgatory (Session 7), keeps CVC goals honest (Sessions 5–6), forces clarity on IP and exclusivity (Sessions 9–10), gives boundary spanners something concrete to push through procurement (Session 11), and makes the partnership survive a champion leaving (Session 12). Most failed collaborations we studied had good technology and good intentions — what they lacked was a shared, written definition of 'this worked'.
followUps: Can you give an example of a success definition that was too vague?
Who should own the success definition — the startup or the corporate?
